rounds.text: Tejnaksh Healthcare Ltd trades at an attractive valuation relative to its sector, offering a P/E of 18.7x and a P/B of 1.00x compared to sector benchmarks of 30.53x and 3.05x respectively [E1, E2, E6, E7]. The company exhibits robust balance sheet health, operating with a debt-to-equity ratio of just 0.01x, minimal borrowings of Rs 0.19 Cr, and a highly comfortable current ratio of 8.41x [E37, E38, E39]. Operational cash generation is exceptionally strong, backed by a cash conversion ratio of 1.46x and free cash flow of Rs 1.21 Cr in March 2026, while completed capital work-in-progress indicates new capacity coming online [E34, E36, E40]. Recent operational metrics demonstrate a sharp turnaround, highlighted by a quarterly operating margin expansion of 6 percentage points year-over-year and results showing accelerating net profit growth of 94% YoY [E31, E60, E67]. Furthermore, the business benefits from a supportive macro healthcare tailwind score of +0.76 and a stable promoter holding of 73.83% [E41, E66]. Conceded: the company has delivered poor historical sales growth and low returns on equity over the past three to five years [E15, E16, E55].

The evidence demonstrates a persistent and structural deterioration in top-line growth across multiple timeframes, with compounded sales shrinking by 3% over 5 years, 4% over 3 years, and 9% over the trailing twelve months [E15, E16, E17]. This contraction is mirrored at the bottom line, where compounded profit growth has declined by 10% over both 5 and 3 years, and by 11% over the trailing twelve months [E19, E20, E21], accompanied by a zero dividend yield [E4]. Operational efficiency metrics also highlight weakness, as evidenced by a low return on equity of 4.7% [E13] and a return on capital employed of just 6.3% [E12], which significantly lag sector benchmarks of 10.16% and 11.62% respectively [E9, E10]. Furthermore, working capital friction is intensifying, shown by debtor days jumping from 48.0 to 75.5 days and overall working capital days expanding from 59.0 to 91.8 days [E56, E57]. Valuation models flag substantial downside risk, with a discounted cash flow intrinsic value of Rs 8 per share pointing to a massive margin of safety deficit of -64.7% against the current market price of Rs 13.8 [E44, E45]. Conceded: the company maintains a strong short-term liquidity profile with a current ratio of 8.41x and is nearly debt-free at 0.01x debt to equity [E37, E38].

The bear’s focus on historical sales and profit contraction [E15, E16, E17, E19, E20, E21] ignores the most recent, high-impact evidence of a fundamental turnaround, specifically the 94% year-over-year surge in net profit and a 6 percentage point expansion in quarterly operating margins [E31, E60]. While the bear highlights lagging long-term ROE and ROCE [E12, E13], it fails to account for the fact that capital expenditure is now largely complete, as evidenced by the 100% reduction in capital work in progress [E40]. This transition from investment to operational execution is already yielding strong cash flow, with profits fully backed by cash at a 1.46x conversion rate [E34, E36]. Conceded: the company has delivered poor long-term sales growth and currently offers no dividend [E4, E54, E53]. Furthermore, the bear’s reliance on a DCF model [E44, E45] is contradicted by the company’s superior valuation metrics, which trade at a significant discount to sector benchmarks, including a P/B of 0.99x versus 3.05x and an EV/EBITDA of 7.69x versus 16.64x [E7, E11]. By focusing on stale historical trends rather than the accelerating quarterly performance and robust balance sheet, the bear misses the inflection point currently underway [E37, E38, E67].

The bull’s reliance on a single quarter of margin expansion [E31] and profit growth [E60] ignores the persistent, multi-year trend of structural decline, including compounded sales growth of -9% over the trailing twelve months [E17] and -3% over five years [E15]. While the bull points to completed capital expenditure [E40], this has not translated into efficient returns, as the company continues to suffer from a low ROCE of 6.35% compared to the sector benchmark of 11.62% [E10]. Conceded: the company has reduced debt [E39, E50] and maintains a comfortable current ratio [E38]. However, the bull’s dismissal of the DCF valuation [E44, E45] is dangerous, as the market price already implies an optimistic 6.8% earnings growth that the company’s historical performance—marked by consistent profit contraction [E19, E20, E21]—has failed to justify [E46]. Furthermore, the bull ignores the deteriorating efficiency of the business, specifically the increase in debtor days from 48.0 to 75.5 and working capital days from 59.0 to 91.8 [E56, E57]. These operational headwinds, combined with a 0% dividend yield [E4, E53], suggest that the current valuation is not a bargain but a reflection of long-term value destruction.
